title: Timeouts do not seem to be used when a connection is aged out
body:
### I did this

libcurl built for an embedded ia-32 system, which is more or less NetBSD 6.0.1. We, so far, have had defaults for connection ages but in a "cloud" environment we have connections that never resolve, blocking that thread for 300s. It appears to be a resolver issue of some kind.

The very next connection to the same host will usually work very quickly. In an attempt to solve this, we set timeouts on the connection via options:

curl_easy_setopt(session.curl, CURLOPT_CONNECTTIMEOUT, 10L);
curl_easy_setopt(session.curl, CURLOPT_TIMEOUT, 20L);

(We tried with and without CURLOPT_NOSIGNAL, and with and without the async resolver.)

And implemented a app-level retry. The idea is that we know the next attempt will almost certainly work immediately. We want to bail out whatever it is doing now and immediately retry.

We see this with NOSIGNAL=1L using the async resolver (but the pattern is very similar with the synchronous resolver):

10:19:04 DEBUG [NotificationServiceThread] HttpClient:435: cURL request #1 to 'https://gcp-ds2.fnord.org:443/rest/thing/getThings'
== Info: Too old connection (121922 ms idle, max idle is 118000 ms), disconnect it
== Info: Connection 1 seems to be dead
== Info: shutting down connection #1
[...]
== Info: connection has input pending, not reusable
== Info: Connection 0 seems to be dead
== Info: shutting down connection #0
== Info: Failed to resolve host 'gcp-ds2.fnord.org' with timeout after 486894 ms
== Info: closing connection #2
10:27:11 DEBUG [NotificationServiceThread] HttpClient:437: cURL request finished (28)
10:27:11 DEBUG [NotificationServiceThread] HttpClient:435: cURL request #2 to 'https://gcp-ds2.fnord.org:443/rest/thing/getThings'
== Info: Host gcp-ds2.fnord.org:443 was resolved.
== Info: IPv6: (none)
== Info: IPv4: 35.237.117.40
== Info:   Trying 35.237.117.40:443...
== Info: SSL reusing session with ALPN '-'
== Info: SSL connection using TLSv1.3 / TLS13-AES256-GCM-SHA384
== Info: Connected to gcp-ds2.fnord.org (35.237.117.40) port 443
== Info: using HTTP/1.x

### I expected the following

Ideally we figure out why it needs to block for minutes resolving. Alternatively, I'd expect the timeout settings to actually timeout so the app-level retry can work.

### curl/libcurl version

curl 8.14.1 and 8.15.0

### operating system

Custom embedded, based on 32-bit Intel NetBSD 6.0.1

comments.author: reporter
reporter
comments.body:
Full disclosure: this is a multi-threaded app, and each thread that needs cURL has thread-local storage for the cURL handle. The handle is created on demand (and recreated if something has gone badly wrong) and "reused" handles are curl_easy_reset() before next use and applying options.

I mention this because I tried simply forcing connections to be closed and never reused but I think our careful threading model is not compatible with this and I'll have to refactor a bit. So I have not done that yet.

I also forget to mention we exclusively use the easy interface -- we have multiple threads doing HTTPS to select hosts.

comments.author: participant1
comments.body: We fixed a DNS timeout issue with c-ares in #18217 recently. That triggered when either redirects occurred or easy handles were reused. Do you run a curl build with c-ares for resolving? Then it might be worth testing that patch.

comments.author: participant2
comments.body: With the threaded or c-ares resolver, the timeout should should be fairly accurate and libcurl does not use signals for that.

comments.author: reporter
comments.body:
> We fixed a DNS timeout issue with c-ares in [#18217](https://github.com/curl/curl/pull/18217) recently. That triggered when either redirects occurred or easy handles were reused. Do you run a curl build with c-ares for resolving? Then it might be worth testing that patch.

I saw that but we do not use c-ares. I can link with it but I didn't want to go all in on a third-party where most of the documentation is about running it on a system as a resolver, not how client libraries use it as a library. On embedded, every library is a potential landmine so I'm not in a hurry to go off on in that direction.

Basically, I have almost no way of adjusting the resolver settings on the embedded device. I can add up to 3 upstream resolvers or accept the DHCP provided ones. But no access to anything resembling a resolv.conf file. And, of course, when it works, it works great.

comments.author: reporter
comments.body:
> With the threaded or c-ares resolver, the timeout should should be fairly accurate and libcurl does not use signals for that.

If CURLOPT_CONNECTTIMEOUT was working I'd be satisfied. But there is something about stale connection retries, this platform, talking to a Google cloud, that is causing the connection to stall for minutes.

Our "on premise" testing does not show this problem (another detail I should have made clear); or at least we didn't get these stale connection leads to stalled next connection issues.

comments.author: reporter
comments.body:
I am experimenting with enabling CURLOPT_TCP_KEEPALIVE and setting curl_easy_setopt(session.curl, CURLOPT_TCP_KEEPIDLE, 30L). I think this means in most cases a connection will likely never get stale. This is a pretty select client-server chat so maybe we are rubbing up against mysterious Google firewalling.

Also, I enabled "alt-svc" because I see Google is actually sending this header. I tend to remove most features from libraries but if the peer wants to use it, I'll leave it in. No idea if that had an impact, or what it might change :)

comments.author: participant1
comments.body:
In the threaded resolver, we detect the timeout from the curl thread, but then wait for the thread to finish. If `getaddrinfo()` hangs, curl will also hang here - as I read the code. I will investigate more tomorrow.

When synchronous resolving, we set an ALARM when available on the platform, which cancels the resolve call. This works nicely on the platform we test. But if there is no ALARM signalling, the timeout will not apply.

I added tracing for this in #18253. To get dns tracing information, you can call `curl_global_trace("dns");` right after global init.

comments.body:
Somehow, curl's configure does not detect support for interrupting `getaddrinfo()` on your platform. The conditions in curl are

```c
#if defined(CURLRES_SYNCH) &&                   \
  defined(HAVE_ALARM) &&                        \
  defined(SIGALRM) &&                           \
  defined(HAVE_SIGSETJMP) &&                    \
  defined(GLOBAL_INIT_IS_THREADSAFE)
/* alarm-based timeouts can only be used with all the dependencies satisfied */
#define USE_ALARM_TIMEOUT
#endif
```
which was last changed in 2023 by adding `GLOBAL_INIT_IS_THREADSAFE`.

We'll need to track down why this is not working as we need it to.

Not sure what you mean, but each of our threads is more or less an infinite task runner until shutdown. It is asked to make a request, does the request, and handles successes and error all within that task until going back into checking for the next time it needs to do some work.

Each task runner has its own CURL handle in its thread local storage which is retrieves (or creates and stores in thread local storage) when it is asked to make a request.

comments.author: participant2
comments.body:
When curl, using the threaded-resolver, starts to resolve a name it starts a new thread for this purpose in which it calls `getaddrinfo()`. When that takes a long time and it times out, curl tries to tell that to stop with pthread_cancel, but it cannot forcible stop the resolver thread. The main thread can then return error and say "timeout" and everything. The child thread could then still be running.

If you then, using the same handle, start a second transfer and the *old* resolver-thread is still running, something needs to be done. To prevent you from just getting more child threads with hanging resolvers, it will "join" the thread before starting a new one, which means waiting until that first resolve fails. Which in your case seems to take a long time.

Ok, so your comment was informational, not something I can act on.

There is another thread that does some work every 2m forever, and it seems to be just sneaking in before the connection is expired and is able to reuse the connection. This is to a different host, and is happening while that other thread is stalled.

So, it is looking like we have the following options:

1. Live with it as a application known issue on this cloud provider.
2. Find another solution other than cURL; either homegrown or some other library. Since we only need HTTP (well, I might have had a future opportunity for telnet and FTP but it is what it is) maybe there is something else we can find or write.
3. See if the sync resolver, possibly with some kind of signal handling gives us better results.
4. Walk back the per-thread handles, closing all connections full, and recreating everything from scratch on every request. We are hoping that a new handle will not run into this problem as we ~~usually~~ only see the problem when a connection is expired.

(3) is a gamble. (4) is probably the best way to continue to use cURL. (2) is the most application work, but we have isolated cURL into a single compilation unit. (1) is hoping we don't see this in the wild very much because maybe its configuration we are getting wrong in our QA, and maybe a long wait is ok for some results or a retry.

In terms of tuning I suppose I can make connections last longer than 118s. We will have at most a handful of hosts in the pool. This pushes the problem to uses after a long idle time. This more or less fixes the problem for QA only I suppose.
